text: A threat model built for a conventional web application asks who can reach an endpoint and what data it touches. Those questions still matter for an AI system, but they miss the risks specific to the model itself. An AI-specific threat model has to add three more dimensions on top.

First, data sensitivity — not just the database, but what the model was trained or fine-tuned on, what it retrieves at query time, and what it might memorize and later reproduce. Second, autonomy level — is this a read-only chatbot that only returns text, or an agent that can call tools and take real actions? The blast radius of an attack scales directly with autonomy. Third, the user trust boundary — who's allowed to talk to this system, and at what trust level. An internal tool used by vetted employees has a very different threat model from a public chatbot anyone can prompt.

STRIDE is Microsoft's established threat-modeling framework — spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege. It wasn't written for AI, but each category maps onto a concrete risk once you know where to look: tampering becomes prompt injection or data poisoning, information disclosure becomes system-prompt leakage or training-data memorization, and elevation of privilege becomes an agent's tool-calling ability being manipulated beyond its intended authority.

Walk it through a real system: a support chatbot that retrieves from an internal knowledge base and can call a create-refund-ticket API. The knowledge base may hold customer data, so retrieval and memorization both matter. It's not read-only — it can create a real ticket — so elevation of privilege is a live concern. Any logged-in customer can prompt it, a wide and unvetted population. Running STRIDE against this system surfaces the real question: can injected content from a retrieved document trigger an unauthorized refund ticket?

That worked example is exactly what a threat model is for — it tells a red-team engagement where to concentrate its test cases instead of testing everything equally. Next, you'll see the organizational governance layer this threat model ultimately feeds into: the real frameworks and regulation that require this kind of documented risk analysis in the first place.
